title: Impact of School Finance Reform on Math Test Scores

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID).

Rationale  
• Schools in reform states (“treated = 1”) are compared with schools in non-reform states (“treated = 0”) before and after the reform (“post = 1”).  
• The coefficient on the interaction treat_x_post (or treated × post) captures the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT).

Key Assumptions  
1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of reform, mean test-score trends for treated and control schools would have moved in parallel.  
2. No Anticipation: Treated schools do not change behavior before the reform takes effect.  
3. Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA): No spillovers between treated and control schools.  
4. Composition Stability: No systematic entry/exit of students or schools correlated with treatment status.

## 2. R Code
```r
##############################
# Difference-in-Differences: #
# School Finance Reform ---> Math Scores
##############################

# 0. Packages ----------------------------------------------------------
libs <- c("readr", "dplyr", "fixest", "sandwich", "lmtest")
invisible(lapply(libs, require, character.only = TRUE))

# 1. Read data ---------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s35_data.csv",
               col_types = cols(
                 unit_id = col_integer(),
                 period  = col_integer(),
                 treated = col_integer(),
                 post    = col_integer(),
                 treat_x_post = col_integer(),
                 y       = col_double()
               ))

# 2. Descriptive statistics -------------------------------------------
cat("N obs =", nrow(df), "\n",
    "Treated schools =", length(unique(df$unit_id[df$treated==1])), "\n",
    "Control schools =", length(unique(df$unit_id[df$treated==0])), "\n")

# 3. Baseline DID ------------------------------------------------------
did_base <- feols(y ~ treated*post | period,         # period FE
                  data = df, cluster = ~unit_id)     # cluster at school level
summary(did_base)

cat("\nBaseline DID estimate (ATT):",
    round(coef(did_base)["treated:post"], 4), "\n")

# 4. TWFE (school & time FE) ------------------------------------------
did_twfe <- feols(y ~ treated:post | unit_id + period,
                  data = df, cluster = ~unit_id)
summary(did_twfe)

cat("\nTWFE DID estimate (ATT):",
    round(coef(did_twfe)["treated:post"], 4), "\n")

# 5. Robustness check 1: School-specific linear trends -----------------
df <- df %>% group_by(unit_id) %>% 
  mutate(t = period - min(period)) %>% ungroup()

did_trend <- feols(y ~ treated:post + i(t, unit_id) | unit_id + period,
                   data = df, cluster = ~unit_id)
cat("\nDID with school-specific linear trends (ATT):",
    round(coef(did_trend)["treated:post"], 4), "\n")

# 6. Robustness check 2: Placebo test (PRE-period only) ----------------
pre_df <- df %>% filter(post == 0)                   # only pre-reform years
placebo <- feols(y ~ treated*t | period,            # fictitious “post” = t>median?
                 data = pre_df, cluster = ~unit_id)
cat("\nPlacebo interaction coefficient (should be ~0):",
    round(coef(placebo)["treated:t"], 4), "\n")

# 7. Event-study visualization (optional) ------------------------------
# Estimates leads & lags with Sun & Abraham
event <- feols(y ~ sunab(treated, period) | unit_id + period,
               data = df, cluster = ~unit_id)
iplot(event, ref.line = 0, xlab = "Years relative to reform",
      main = "Event-study: Finance reform & math scores")
```

The script:  
1. Loads the CSV, prints basic sample counts.  
2. Baseline DID with time fixed effects.  
3. Two-way fixed effects (school & time).  
4. Adds school-specific linear trends.  
5. Conducts a placebo (pre-period only) test.  
6. Optionally plots an event-study for visual pre-trend inspection.  
All key coefficients are printed in the console.

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive. Greater state funding should let schools hire better teachers, reduce class size, or buy learning materials—raising math scores.  

Magnitude: Education interventions often yield 0.05–0.10 standard-deviation gains in the short run. I therefore expect an ATT of roughly +0.07 SD (±0.03). Robustness checks should show similar positive effects, while the placebo coefficient should hover around zero, supporting the parallel-trends assumption.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: We compare changes in math test scores over time between schools affected by the reform and those that were not.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The reform led to a decrease in math test scores.
